lead: A regular expression is a formula that describes a language. Two different formulas can describe the same language. Algebraic laws for regular expressions are equations that let you replace one formula by an equal one, without drawing an automaton. They are used to simplify patterns, to prove that two patterns match the same strings, and to clean up expressions produced by automaton-to-regex conversions. The laws mirror ordinary algebra in some places and differ sharply in others: union is idempotent, concatenation is not commutative, and star has its own rules. Only a few universities teach this as a named topic.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the operators, precedence and the meaning of ∅, ε and Kleene star.

blocks.text: Write r, s and t for regular expressions, and L(r) for the language of r. An identity r = s means L(r) = L(s): both sides match the same strings. Here + is union, juxtaposition is concatenation, and * is Kleene star.
r + s = s + r,  (r + s) + t = r + (s + t),  r + r = r,  r + ∅ = r
blocks.where: r, s, t are regular expressions; + is union; ∅ is the empty language, containing no string.

blocks.text: Concatenation has identity ε and annihilator ∅: εr = rε = r and ∅r = r∅ = ∅. Here ε is the string of length zero. Concatenation is associative: (rs)t = r(st). It distributes over union: r(s + t) = rs + rt and (s + t)r = sr + tr.
The star laws are the ones students miss. (r*)* = r*, ε + rr* = r*, and (r + s)* = (r*s*)*. Also ∅* = ε and ε* = ε. Starring any language includes the empty string, so these last two are expected.
Simplify by applying one law per step and naming it. Drop ∅ from unions. Drop ε from concatenations. Collapse double stars. Replace ε + rr* by r* when the union has ε and a starred copy.

items: Apply one reducing law and name it.
Repeat while any law changes the expression.
Test short strings on both sides.

blocks.text: Union is idempotent: r + r = r. There is no coefficient 2. Writing r + r = 2r is wrong because 2r is not a regular expression here. Also r + ε is not r in general; it adds the empty string.

The figure after this section uses these moves on (ε + a)*. The first rewrite is the union-star law; then ε* becomes ε; then ε is removed by the concatenation identity; finally the double star collapses. Check every step against the language, not against arithmetic.

Each law is a set statement. For r + r = r, a string is in L(r + r) exactly when it is in L(r) or in L(r), which is the same as being in L(r). For ∅r = ∅, no string can split into a part from ∅ and a part from r, because the first part cannot exist.

For (r + s)* = (r*s*)*, group consecutive pieces from r and from s into alternating blocks. Each block lies in r* or s*, so the whole string lies in (r*s*)*. Conversely, r* and s* use only r and s, so every string in (r*s*)* lies in (r + s)*.
These laws shorten expressions before conversion to an automaton in Chapter 2.3 and after conversion from a DFA in Chapter 2.4. They also support language equality proofs.

figure.caption: Four laws turn (ε + a)* into a*: the union-star law gives (ε* a*)*, then ε* = ε, ε drops out of the concatenation, and the double star collapses, leaving zero or more a’s.

spec.aria: A vertical chain of five expressions from (ε + a)* to a*, each arrow labelled with the law it uses: (r + s)* = (r* s*)*, ε* = ε, ε r = r and (r*)* = r*.

examples.question: Simplify (ε + a)* using algebraic laws. Name each law used.
steps: Apply (r + s)* = (r*s*)* with r = ε and s = a: (ε* a*)*.
Apply εr = r with r = a*: (a*)*.
Apply (r*)* = r* with r = a: a*.
examples.answer: Both (ε + a)* and a* describe the same language: all strings of zero or more a's.

traps: r + r = r, not 2r. This algebra has no coefficients.
∅ and ε are different: ∅ has no strings, ε has one empty string. r + ∅ = r, but r + ε adds ε.
Concatenation is not commutative: ab ≠ ba in general.
Star binds tightest, and (r + s)* is not r* + s*. For example, ab is in (a + b)* but not in a* + b*.

quiz.q: State the identity law for union with ∅.
Why is r + r = r true for languages?
quiz.a: A string is in L(r + r) exactly when it is in L(r) or in L(r), which is the same as being in L(r).

quiz.q: Simplify (ε + b)* and name two laws used.
A student writes (a + b)* = a* + b*. Give one string in the left side not in the right.
quiz.a: ab is in (a + b)* but not in a* + b*. The right side contains only all-a strings or all-b strings.
∅; concatenation with the empty language gives no strings.
a(ε + b*) = a b*, because ε + b* = b*.

beyond: Not for the exam. These identities form Kleene algebra, an algebraic system used to reason about programs and regular languages. Regex engines and lexer generators apply similar rewrites to make patterns shorter or faster. Search next for Kleene algebra, regular-expression equivalence and regex simplification.
